title: The 1973–74 Oil Crisis and Global Financial Shock
region: Middle East; United States; Western Europe; Japan; India
category: Oil shock, inflation and global recession
lede: The Yom Kippur War was followed by an Arab oil embargo and production cuts that quadrupled oil prices, transferring income to oil exporters and imposing inflationary and recessionary pressure on oil-importing economies.
overview: On 6 October 1973, Egypt and Syria launched a surprise attack on Israel, beginning the Yom Kippur War. Following U.S. resupply of Israel, Arab members of OAPEC announced an embargo against the United States and selected other countries and cut production. The shock interacted with pre-existing oil-market tensions and limited spare capacity. Oil prices rose from about US$2.90 per barrel before the embargo to US$11.65 in January 1974. The embargo was lifted in March 1974, but the price shock remained. This episode is often called the first oil shock; it should not be conflated with the separate 1979–80 oil shock.
humanImpact: Oil-importing economies experienced fuel shortages, higher transport and production costs, inflation and recessionary pressure. In the United States, fuel rationing and queues became visible; the United Kingdom introduced a three-day working week during the winter energy crisis. Japan and Western European economies faced major import-cost pressure. India's RBI historical chronology records quadrupled oil prices, double-digit inflation and a global recession. Oil exporters experienced a large increase in export revenues. These outcomes varied by country and policy response.

title: The Asian Financial Crisis
region: Bangkok, Thailand; Jakarta, Indonesia; Seoul, South Korea; Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia; wider East and Southeast Asia
lede: A currency crisis that began with Thailand's decision to float the baht spread through several Asian economies, exposing vulnerabilities in foreign borrowing, exchange-rate regimes and financial institutions.
overview: The crisis developed after pressure on Thailand's baht intensified. On 2 July 1997, authorities allowed the currency to float. Contagion and investor reassessment affected Indonesia, Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines and other markets, although each economy had different vulnerabilities and policy responses.
humanImpact: The crisis brought recession, unemployment, financial-sector restructuring and hardship for households and workers. IMF retrospective material records a fall of more than 10% in Thailand's real GDP in 1998. Country-level effects should be explored separately rather than treated as identical across Asia.

title: The Dot-Com Bubble Burst (2000–2002)
lede: Technology shares peaked on 10 March 2000 before a prolonged collapse in internet and technology valuations. The Nasdaq Composite fell about 77% from its peak by October 2002, as speculative business models, high valuations and financing conditions unwound.
overview: Technology shares peaked on 10 March 2000 before a prolonged collapse in internet and technology valuations. The Nasdaq Composite fell about 77% from its peak by October 2002, as speculative business models, high valuations and financing conditions unwound. The episode exposed the risks of valuing growth companies on expectations without durable earnings or cash flows. The repricing affected venture funding, IPO markets, technology employment and equity portfolios.
humanImpact: The technology-company concentration around Silicon Valley and the trading and capital-raising ecosystem in New York were two important nodes; the repricing spread internationally.

title: The Global Financial Crisis (2007–2009)
lede: Stress in U.S. subprime mortgage markets and structured-credit products escalated from 2007 into a global banking and economic crisis. Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on 15 September 2008, and governments and central banks intervened to contain systemic disruption.
overview: Stress in U.S. subprime mortgage markets and structured-credit products escalated from 2007 into a global banking and economic crisis. Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on 15 September 2008, and governments and central banks intervened to contain systemic disruption. High leverage, weak underwriting, securitisation complexity and fragile wholesale funding transmitted housing losses through interconnected financial institutions.
humanImpact: New York was a centre of major financial institutions and markets; Washington, D.C. was the centre of federal crisis response. The crisis spread through banking, trade and capital flows worldwide.

title: The 2026 Iran War, Strait of Hormuz Disruption and Global Oil Shock
region: Persian Gulf; Middle East; Asia; Europe; global energy markets
category: Geopolitical oil shock and global supply-chain disruption
lede: The war involving Iran, Israel and the United States disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, triggering a major oil and gas supply shock whose effects travelled through energy-importing economies, freight networks and financial markets.
overview: On 28 February 2026, the United States and Israel began military strikes against Iran. Iran retaliated across the region, and traffic through the Strait of Hormuz—normally carrying roughly one-fifth to one-quarter of seaborne oil and petroleum-product trade—fell sharply. The disruption affected crude, refined products and LNG exports from the Gulf. Emergency stock releases, rerouting through bypass infrastructure, increased output elsewhere and weaker demand cushioned the shock, but did not immediately restore normal flows. By September, the IEA reported renewed upward price pressure as hostilities persisted and inventories had fallen. In early November, oil prices fell sharply amid hopes of de-escalation and signs of recovering exports, though shipping attacks and the lack of a comprehensive settlement kept risk elevated.
humanImpact: The disruption raised uncertainty and costs for households, transport operators, airlines, manufacturers and governments. Oil-importing Asian economies—including India, Japan, South Korea and China—were especially exposed to Gulf supply and price changes. Gulf exporters faced interrupted shipments and risks to infrastructure. European and Asian refining, trading and shipping hubs faced higher freight, insurance and product-market volatility. The effects differed by country and over time: the map marks important energy nodes and economic exposure centres, not identical levels of direct damage.

title: The Mexican Peso Crisis (1994–1995)
lede: In December 1994, Mexico devalued the peso after pressure on foreign-exchange reserves and the exchange-rate regime. Capital outflows, short-term dollar-linked public debt and declining confidence intensified the crisis. The peso fell sharply, financing conditions tightened and the shock spread to other emerging markets, becoming known as the Tequila Crisis.
overview: In December 1994, Mexico devalued the peso after pressure on foreign-exchange reserves and the exchange-rate regime. Capital outflows, short-term dollar-linked public debt and declining confidence intensified the crisis. The peso fell sharply, financing conditions tightened and the shock spread to other emerging markets, becoming known as the Tequila Crisis. The crisis showed how a fixed or tightly managed exchange-rate commitment can become vulnerable when reserves, fiscal credibility, short-term financing and investor confidence come under pressure. The structure of short-term dollar-linked debt made refinancing particularly difficult.
humanImpact: Mexico faced recession, inflation and a severe squeeze on household purchasing power. Banks and businesses came under stress, while the United States and international institutions arranged emergency support. The episode also triggered wider reassessment of emerging-market risk.

title: The Asian Financial Crisis (1997–1998)
region: Bangkok, Thailand; Jakarta, Indonesia; Seoul, South Korea; Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia
lede: The crisis began when Thailand abandoned its baht-dollar peg on 2 July 1997. Currency pressure and investor reassessment spread through Indonesia, South Korea, Malaysia and other regional markets. Foreign-currency borrowing, short-term external debt, weak financial institutions and fragile exchange-rate arrangements amplified the shock. The crisis continued through 1998 and had spillovers beyond Asia.
overview: The crisis began when Thailand abandoned its baht-dollar peg on 2 July 1997. Currency pressure and investor reassessment spread through Indonesia, South Korea, Malaysia and other regional markets. Foreign-currency borrowing, short-term external debt, weak financial institutions and fragile exchange-rate arrangements amplified the shock. The crisis continued through 1998 and had spillovers beyond Asia. The episode demonstrated how currency mismatches, leveraged borrowing and fragile banking systems can turn pressure on one currency into a regional financial crisis. National experiences and policy responses differed; the crisis was not a single identical event across every country.
humanImpact: Businesses failed, banks were restructured, currencies depreciated and output contracted. Households experienced job losses and reduced incomes. The crisis also reshaped regional financial regulation, reserve management and debates about IMF crisis programmes.

title: The Russian Financial Crisis & LTCM Collapse (1998)
lede: Russia devalued the rouble, restructured domestic government debt and declared a moratorium on some private external debt payments in August 1998. The turmoil caused investors to flee riskier assets. Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM), a highly leveraged hedge fund with large positions across global markets, suffered severe losses as normally related prices moved sharply apart. A private-sector recapitalisation was organised with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York facilitating discussions.
overview: Russia devalued the rouble, restructured domestic government debt and declared a moratorium on some private external debt payments in August 1998. The turmoil caused investors to flee riskier assets. Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM), a highly leveraged hedge fund with large positions across global markets, suffered severe losses as normally related prices moved sharply apart. A private-sector recapitalisation was organised with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York facilitating discussions. The episode illustrated how sovereign risk, market liquidity and highly leveraged financial institutions can interact. Positions that appear diversified under normal conditions may become correlated during a crisis, while forced selling can intensify market stress.
humanImpact: Russian households and businesses faced inflation, financial disruption and loss of confidence. International markets experienced a flight to quality and wider credit spreads. The LTCM episode intensified scrutiny of leverage, counterparty exposures and systemic risk.

title: The Enron Corporate Accounting Scandal (2001)
lede: Enron disclosed a large quarterly loss in October 2001 and revealed accounting issues that undermined confidence in its reported earnings and financial position. The company had used complex structures and accounting practices to obscure debt and inflate performance. It filed for bankruptcy in December 2001, then the largest U.S. corporate bankruptcy at the time.
overview: Enron disclosed a large quarterly loss in October 2001 and revealed accounting issues that undermined confidence in its reported earnings and financial position. The company had used complex structures and accounting practices to obscure debt and inflate performance. It filed for bankruptcy in December 2001, then the largest U.S. corporate bankruptcy at the time. The scandal exposed weaknesses in corporate governance, auditor independence, disclosure and the oversight of off-balance-sheet entities. It showed how investors can be misled when financial statements do not present a clear picture of a company's obligations and risks.
humanImpact: Employees lost jobs and retirement savings, shareholders suffered major losses, and confidence in corporate reporting was damaged. The scandal helped drive the Sarbanes–Oxley Act of 2002 and tighter requirements for audit committees, internal controls and financial disclosures.

title: The Argentine Debt Default & Peso Devaluation (2001–2002)
lede: After years of recession and mounting debt pressures, Argentina defaulted on sovereign debt in December 2001. In early 2002 it abandoned the currency-board arrangement that had pegged the peso one-to-one with the U.S. dollar. The peso depreciated sharply, bank withdrawals were restricted and the financial system suffered a deep crisis.
overview: After years of recession and mounting debt pressures, Argentina defaulted on sovereign debt in December 2001. In early 2002 it abandoned the currency-board arrangement that had pegged the peso one-to-one with the U.S. dollar. The peso depreciated sharply, bank withdrawals were restricted and the financial system suffered a deep crisis. The crisis reflected an increasingly unsustainable exchange-rate arrangement, rising public debt, weak growth and reduced access to external financing. The sudden end of convertibility exposed the risks of trying to maintain a currency peg without a supporting fiscal and economic framework.
humanImpact: Output and incomes collapsed, poverty rose and savings were disrupted. Banks, businesses and households faced severe uncertainty as deposits and contracts were affected by emergency measures. The crisis became a major case study in sovereign debt restructuring and exchange-rate regimes.

overview: In June 2012, Barclays agreed to major regulatory settlements after investigations found that traders and submitters had attempted to manipulate submissions used to calculate the London Interbank Offered Rate (Libor). humanImpact: The case damaged public trust in banks and prompted criminal and regulatory investigations, fines and reforms to benchmark administration. Libor was subsequently phased out in major currencies and replaced by alternative reference rates.

title: The Swiss Franc De-pegging Shock (2015)
lede: On 15 January 2015, the Swiss National Bank unexpectedly discontinued its minimum exchange rate of CHF 1.20 per euro and lowered interest rates. The franc appreciated sharply, causing extreme volatility and losses for some leveraged currency traders and brokers.
overview: On 15 January 2015, the Swiss National Bank unexpectedly discontinued its minimum exchange rate of CHF 1.20 per euro and lowered interest rates. The franc appreciated sharply, causing extreme volatility and losses for some leveraged currency traders and brokers. The minimum exchange rate had required sustained intervention as the euro weakened. The SNB concluded that maintaining the floor was no longer sustainable in the changed international environment. The abrupt policy change left markets little time to adjust.
humanImpact: The franc's rapid appreciation affected exporters, tourism businesses and investors. Some retail foreign-exchange brokers suffered heavy losses, highlighting the risks of leverage, thin liquidity and sudden central-bank policy changes.

title: The Yen Carry Trade Unwind Market Panic (2024)
lede: In early August 2024, global markets experienced a sharp bout of volatility as leveraged positions were unwound. A stronger yen and changing expectations about Japanese and U.S. interest rates contributed to pressure on carry trades, while weaker-than-expected U.S. economic data intensified the sell-off. Japanese equities recorded an exceptionally sharp one-day fall on 5 August before markets stabilised.
overview: In early August 2024, global markets experienced a sharp bout of volatility as leveraged positions were unwound. A stronger yen and changing expectations about Japanese and U.S. interest rates contributed to pressure on carry trades, while weaker-than-expected U.S. economic data intensified the sell-off. Japanese equities recorded an exceptionally sharp one-day fall on 5 August before markets stabilised. A yen carry trade typically involves borrowing in a low-interest-rate currency to invest in higher-yielding assets elsewhere. When the funding currency strengthens or interest-rate expectations change, investors may close positions quickly, amplifying price movements across markets.
humanImpact: The Nikkei experienced a historic one-day decline, global equity markets fell and volatility spiked. The episode highlighted how leverage, crowded trades and currency movements can connect markets across countries.

overview: On 7 January 2009, Satyam's chairman disclosed that the company's accounts had been falsified over several years, including inflated cash balances and profits. The admission shocked investors and raised questions about audit quality, board oversight and corporate governance in India's technology sector. The fraud showed how fabricated financial statements can mislead investors, lenders and employees when independent verification, audit challenge and board oversight fail. It became a major test of India's corporate-governance and enforcement framework.
humanImpact: Satyam's share price collapsed, employees faced uncertainty and investors suffered losses. The government intervened to stabilise the company, which was later acquired by Tech Mahindra. The case prompted renewed scrutiny of auditors and listed-company governance.

title: The Foreign Institutional Investor (FII) “Taper Tantrum” Shock (2013)
region: Washington, D.C., United States; Mumbai, India
lede: In May 2013, Federal Reserve communication about the possible reduction of asset purchases triggered a reassessment of global interest-rate expectations. Portfolio investors withdrew funds from several emerging markets, including India. The rupee came under intense pressure and fell sharply against the U.S. dollar during the following months.
overview: In May 2013, Federal Reserve communication about the possible reduction of asset purchases triggered a reassessment of global interest-rate expectations. Portfolio investors withdrew funds from several emerging markets, including India. The rupee came under intense pressure and fell sharply against the U.S. dollar during the following months. The episode showed how a change in monetary policy expectations in a major reserve-currency economy can redirect global capital flows. India's external vulnerabilities and macroeconomic imbalances amplified the impact of foreign portfolio outflows.
humanImpact: The rupee depreciated sharply, bond yields and market volatility rose, and the RBI introduced measures to stabilise the foreign-exchange market. The episode became a key example of emerging-market exposure to global financial conditions.

title: The PNB–Nirav Modi Banking Fraud (2018)
lede: Punjab National Bank disclosed unauthorised letters of undertaking issued through its Brady House branch in Mumbai. The instruments had been used to obtain credit from overseas branches of other banks without being properly recorded in the bank's core systems. The fraud involved billions of dollars in exposure and triggered investigations.
overview: Punjab National Bank disclosed unauthorised letters of undertaking issued through its Brady House branch in Mumbai. The instruments had been used to obtain credit from overseas branches of other banks without being properly recorded in the bank's core systems. The fraud involved billions of dollars in exposure and triggered investigations. The case exposed failures in internal controls, access management, reconciliation and oversight of trade-finance instruments. It showed how transactions can bypass a bank's normal risk systems when messaging and core banking controls are not integrated.
humanImpact: The disclosure damaged confidence in PNB and raised concerns about governance and controls across the banking sector. Investigations, asset recovery efforts and regulatory scrutiny followed.

title: The Franklin Templeton Mutual Fund Debt Crisis (2020)
lede: In April 2020, Franklin Templeton announced the winding up of six Indian debt mutual-fund schemes, citing severe market dislocation and a lack of liquidity during the COVID-19 shock. Investors could not redeem units in the usual way while the schemes moved into a wind-up process.
overview: In April 2020, Franklin Templeton announced the winding up of six Indian debt mutual-fund schemes, citing severe market dislocation and a lack of liquidity during the COVID-19 shock. Investors could not redeem units in the usual way while the schemes moved into a wind-up process. The episode showed that debt mutual funds are exposed to liquidity risk as well as credit risk. Assets that appear tradable in normal markets can become difficult to sell when many investors seek cash at the same time and buyers disappear.
humanImpact: Investors faced uncertainty and delayed access to their money. The case led to legal proceedings, regulatory scrutiny and debate about liquidity management, valuation and risk disclosures in debt funds.

title: Life Insurance Corporation (LIC) Historic IPO (2022)
lede: LIC's initial public offering opened in May 2022 and became India's largest IPO at the time. The government sold a minority stake in the state-owned insurer as part of its disinvestment programme, while LIC's listing brought a major public financial institution into the listed equity market.
overview: LIC's initial public offering opened in May 2022 and became India's largest IPO at the time. The government sold a minority stake in the state-owned insurer as part of its disinvestment programme, while LIC's listing brought a major public financial institution into the listed equity market. The IPO was significant for India's capital markets, public-sector disinvestment and retail investor participation. It also raised questions about valuation, public ownership and how a large, established insurer should be assessed by listed-market investors.
humanImpact: The offering attracted substantial attention from domestic and international investors and expanded public-market access to LIC shares. The listing became a landmark in India's equity-market history.

title: The Tech Startup Valuation Winter & Governance Crises (2023–2024)
lede: During 2023–2024, tighter global financing conditions and more demanding investor expectations contributed to a reset in startup valuations and funding across India. Several firms cut costs, reduced headcount, delayed listings or faced scrutiny over governance, related-party transactions and accounting practices. The experience varied by company and sector.
overview: During 2023–2024, tighter global financing conditions and more demanding investor expectations contributed to a reset in startup valuations and funding across India. Several firms cut costs, reduced headcount, delayed listings or faced scrutiny over governance, related-party transactions and accounting practices. The experience varied by company and sector. The period highlighted the dependence of high-growth businesses on continued access to external capital, the importance of credible unit economics and the risks of valuing companies mainly on future growth assumptions.
humanImpact: Startups and employees faced layoffs and restructuring, investors reassessed portfolios and founders faced greater pressure to demonstrate sustainable cash flows and governance standards. Bengaluru was one important ecosystem centre, not the only location affected.

title: RBI Regulatory Clampdown on Fintech Payment Gateways (2024)
lede: On 31 January 2024, the RBI directed Paytm Payments Bank to stop accepting fresh deposits, credit transactions and top-ups after 29 February, citing persistent non-compliance and supervisory concerns. The deadline was later extended to 15 March 2024. The action affected customer and merchant payment arrangements linked to the bank.
overview: On 31 January 2024, the RBI directed Paytm Payments Bank to stop accepting fresh deposits, credit transactions and top-ups after 29 February, citing persistent non-compliance and supervisory concerns. The deadline was later extended to 15 March 2024. The action affected customer and merchant payment arrangements linked to the bank. The action underscored that fintech innovation does not remove the need for banking regulation, KYC compliance, operational controls and protection of customer funds. It also distinguished the regulated bank from other parts of the Paytm group.
humanImpact: Customers and merchants had to shift certain banking and payment functions, while the wider fintech sector reassessed compliance and operational dependencies. RBI's action became a major regulatory moment for India's digital-payments ecosystem.

title: Prolonged United States Government Financial Shutdown & Global Market Impact (2025–2026)
lede: A government-wide U.S. funding lapse began on 1 October 2025, at the start of FY2026, and ended when funding legislation was signed on 12 November 2025 after 42 full days. Separate funding lapses followed in 2026: a brief partial lapse in early February and a Department of Homeland Security funding lapse from 14 February to 30 April 2026. These were distinct shutdown episodes, not one continuous government-wide shutdown.
overview: A government-wide U.S. funding lapse began on 1 October 2025, at the start of FY2026, and ended when funding legislation was signed on 12 November 2025 after 42 full days. Separate funding lapses followed in 2026: a brief partial lapse in early February and a Department of Homeland Security funding lapse from 14 February to 30 April 2026. These were distinct shutdown episodes, not one continuous government-wide shutdown. The shutdowns reflected disagreements over appropriations and continuing funding legislation. They affected federal operations, employee pay and public services, while uncertainty about government data releases and spending could complicate economic analysis and market expectations.
humanImpact: The 2025 shutdown was the longest government-wide shutdown on record at the time. The later DHS shutdown was a separate partial shutdown. The funding gaps disrupted services and workers and created uncertainty for businesses and investors; the economic effects varied by agency and duration.
